subject: pharmacology
title: Haematinics: Iron, B12, Folate and Haematopoietic Growth Factors

steps.tx: Oral **ferrous sulfate** remains the reference iron salt: cheap, effective and limited mainly by gastrointestinal tolerance, with roughly 65 mg of elemental iron per 325 mg tablet absorbed best in the ferrous state on an empty stomach. Vitamin C and gastric acid aid uptake while tea, calcium, antacids and proton pump inhibitors obstruct it, so timing around food and other tablets is pharmacology, not fussiness. Alternate day dosing exploits hepcidin rhythms and may absorb better than daily divided doses.
steps.say: Ferrous iron, empty stomach, away from tea and antacids; alternate days can beat daily for absorption.

vis.alt: Systemic iron homeostasis and transport diagram showing absorption, transferrin transport and hepcidin control
vis.caption: Iron homeostasis and transport, the system oral and parenteral iron preparations feed.

steps.tx: Parenteral iron bypasses absorption failure, intolerance, ongoing losses and the need for rapid repletion: **iron sucrose** in small repeated doses, ferric carboxymaltose in large single infusions, and older iron dextran, which uniquely demands a test dose for its higher anaphylaxis history. Modern complexes release iron slowly to transferrin, making serious reactions rare, though hypophosphataemia follows repeated ferric carboxymaltose through FGF23 effects. Haemoglobin rises over two to four weeks whichever route refills the stores.
steps.say: Vein iron skips the gut argument; carboxymaltose gives grams at once, dextran keeps its test dose tradition.

left.title: Oral iron territory
points: Ferrous sulfate, fumarate and gluconate salts
Absorption blocked by tea, calcium and acid suppression
Nausea, constipation and black stools limit adherence
Best for stable patients who absorb and tolerate

right.title: Parenteral iron territory
points: Malabsorption, intolerance or ongoing heavy losses
Ferric carboxymaltose: large single dose infusions
Iron sucrose: smaller repeated doses, dialysis staple
Iron dextran: test dose for anaphylaxis history

steps.tx: The iron chelator **desferrioxamine** (deferoxamine) binds ferric iron for urinary and biliary excretion in transfusional overload of thalassaemia and in acute iron poisoning, where shock and metabolic acidosis make chelation urgent. Given by slow infusion because rapid injection provokes hypotension, its chronic use costs hearing, vision and growth plate surveillance, and it notoriously feeds Yersinia and mucormycosis by donating them captured iron. Oral deferasirox and deferiprone now carry most chronic chelation.
steps.say: Desferrioxamine traps iron for excretion in poisoning and overload; infuse slowly and remember it feeds certain fungi.

nodes.label: Iron overload or acute iron poisoning
Desferrioxamine binds ferric iron in tissues and plasma
Ferrioxamine excreted in urine (vin rose) and bile
Monitor hearing, vision and growth on chronic therapy

steps.tx: **Vitamin B12** (cobalamin, given as cyanocobalamin or hydroxocobalamin) cofactors methionine synthase and methylmalonyl CoA mutase, so deficiency produces megaloblastic anaemia plus subacute combined degeneration of the cord, glossitis and neuropsychiatric features that folate cannot fix. Absorption needs intrinsic factor and terminal ileum, so pernicious anaemia, gastrectomy and ileal disease demand intramuscular replacement, typically loading doses then three monthly maintenance for life when the cause is irreversible.
steps.say: B12 protects cord as well as marrow; when absorption is broken, injections for life are the prescription.

left.title: B12 deficiency clues
points: Megaloblastic anaemia with hypersegmented neutrophils
Subacute combined degeneration: dorsal and lateral columns
Glossitis, cognitive and psychiatric features
Raised methylmalonic acid and homocysteine

right.title: Replacement logic
points: Intramuscular when absorption is the defect
High dose oral can work by passive diffusion
Neurological disease: urgent, frequent loading
Treat before folate to avoid masking, below

steps.tx: **Vitamin B12**, supplied as cyanocobalamin or hydroxocobalamin, is a cofactor for methionine synthase and for methylmalonyl CoA mutase. Deficiency therefore causes megaloblastic anaemia together with subacute combined degeneration of the cord, glossitis and neuropsychiatric illness, and folate does not repair the cord or the mind. Uptake requires intrinsic factor and an intact terminal ileum. Pernicious anaemia, gastrectomy and ileal disease need intramuscular loading and then injections about every three months for life if the cause is permanent.
steps.say: Vitamin B12 supports marrow and spinal cord. Lack of it causes megaloblastic anaemia, cord degeneration, a sore tongue and mental change, none of which folate will correct in the nervous system. Absorption needs intrinsic factor and the terminal ileum. After pernicious anaemia, gastrectomy or ileal loss, injections continue about every three months for life.

vis.alt: A pathway diagram follows vitamin B12 from binding with intrinsic factor to uptake across the terminal ileum.
vis.caption: Cobalamin is shown bound to intrinsic factor and absorbed only when it reaches the terminal ileum. Illustration: StewardMD original.

steps.tx: **Folic acid** treats megaloblastic anaemia of pregnancy, malnutrition, malabsorption and antifolate drugs, and periconception supplementation prevents neural tube defects, the public health triumph of this vitamin. The trap is giving folate alone in undiagnosed megaloblastic anaemia: the blood corrects while B12 neurology silently worsens, so B12 is excluded or treated first. **Folinic acid** (leucovorin) is reduced folate that bypasses dihydrofolate reductase, rescuing marrow from methotrexate and potentiating fluorouracil in oncology regimens.
steps.say: Folate fixes the blood picture and can hide B12 cord damage; folinic acid is the version that bypasses methotrexate's block.

nodes.label: Exclude or treat B12 deficiency first
Folic acid repletes folate stores safely
Folinic acid reserved for antifolate rescue and oncology

steps.tx: Recombinant **erythropoietin** (epoetin) and its long acting cousin darbepoetin, with a half life stretched roughly threefold by extra carbohydrate, replace the renal hormone missing in chronic kidney disease anaemia. Iron stores must be replete first or the marrow cannot answer; haemoglobin targets stay deliberately subnormal (about 10 to 11.5 g per dl) because trials chasing normality bought strokes and clots. Hypertension and pure red cell aplasia from anti erythropoietin antibodies are the named hazards.
steps.say: Replace the kidney's hormone, feed iron first, and aim below normal; chasing normal haemoglobin harmed patients.

left.title: Epoetin and darbepoetin use
points: Chronic kidney disease anaemia the core indication
Iron stores repleted before and during therapy
Darbepoetin dosed weekly to monthly by design
Haemoglobin target deliberately subnormal

right.title: Hazards to police
points: Hypertension and accelerated rises in haemoglobin
Thromboembolism when targets overshoot
Pure red cell aplasia from antibodies, rare
Cancer use restricted by mortality signals

steps.tx: Colony stimulating factors industrialise marrow lineages: **filgrastim** (G CSF, granulocyte colony stimulating factor) shortens chemotherapy neutropenia and mobilises stem cells for harvest, its pegylated form pegfilgrastim stretching one injection across a cycle; sargramostim (GM CSF) broadens to monocytes at the price of capillary leak and fever. Bone pain from an expanding marrow is the everyday adverse effect, splenic rupture the rare catastrophe behind left shoulder tip pain warnings.
steps.say: Filgrastim marches neutrophils back after chemotherapy; bone pain is expected, shoulder tip pain is the alarm.

nodes.label: Filgrastim or pegfilgrastim given after chemotherapy
Neutrophil recovery shortens, febrile neutropenia falls
Bone pain common; splenic rupture rare but warned

steps.tx: Thrombopoiesis has its own pharmacology: oprelvekin (interleukin 11) historically raised platelets amid fluid retention and atrial arrhythmias, while thrombopoietin receptor agonists **romiplostim** (weekly injection) and eltrombopag (oral, chelates with food cations) transformed immune thrombocytopenia by ordering the marrow to manufacture platelets rather than suppressing their destruction. Overshoot thrombocytosis, marrow reticulin and rebound thrombocytopenia on stopping write their monitoring rules, and eltrombopag adds liver enzyme surveillance.
steps.say: Romiplostim and eltrombopag order more platelets instead of defending existing ones; titrate to safe, not normal.

left.title: Thrombopoietin agonists
points: Romiplostim weekly subcutaneous injection
Eltrombopag oral, empty stomach away from cations
Target platelets above 50, not normalisation
Rebound fall below baseline on abrupt stopping

right.title: Older and adjacent agents
points: Oprelvekin (IL 11): fluid retention, arrhythmias, largely historical
Eltrombopag also serves aplastic anaemia and hepatitis C settings
Liver enzymes monitored on eltrombopag
Thrombosis risk rises as counts overshoot
